subtype: Heavy days behind a functioning face [Actor]
passage: "Here's the thing people don't get. I never missed a class. Not one. I'm Lalit, and in my third year I was top of the attendance list and completely empty inside. I'd sit in lectures and hear nothing. At night I was exhausted but couldn't sleep. And the thought that kept coming back was: everyone would be happier if I wasn't around. I didn't say it to anyone. I was scared and ashamed of it. One evening my friend Ira asked, 'You've been somewhere else for weeks. What's going on?' And I just said it. The thought, out loud. Ira didn't panic or lecture. She said, 'Thank you for telling me. You're not a burden. We're going to get help tonight.' She stayed with me, called the campus helpline with me, and walked me to the counsellor first thing next morning. That's why I'm here talking to you."

qa.a: The attendance list.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the thought that kept coming back?
qa.a: Lalit felt scared and ashamed of it and kept it secret.

qa.q: What was the turning point that got Lalit help?
qa.a: Lalit spoke the thought out loud to Ira, who stayed, called the campus helpline with Lalit that night and went to the counsellor next morning.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling when Lalit said the thought out loud?
qa.a: Ira was probably worried and shaken, yet steady enough not to panic, to stay with Lalit and to get help that same night.

subtype: Heavy days behind a functioning face [Actor]
passage: I'm Payal, and I share a flat with Anirban. From the outside he was fine. He went to the office every day, ironed his shirts, smiled at our landlord. I didn't notice much, except that his dinner plate often went back to the fridge untouched, and he slept all Sunday. Last Friday he was washing up and said, very flatly, "Honestly, you'd all be better off without me." I don't know exactly what was in his head. But I didn't let it go. I turned off the tap and said, "I heard that. I'm staying right here with you." We sat on the kitchen floor. I asked if he was safe tonight, and he said he wasn't sure. So I called his brother, and we rang a helpline together. His brother came over and stayed. Next morning we went with him to a doctor.

qa.q: What did Anirban say while washing up?
qa.a: Honestly, you'd all be better off without me.

qa.q: What does Anirban saying he wasn't sure if he was safe suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hopeless and was struggling far more than his daily routine showed.

qa.q: Which of Payal's choices mattered most that night?
qa.a: Payal took his words seriously, stayed with him, asked about his safety, called his brother and a helpline, and went with him to a doctor.

qa.q: How might Anirban's brother have felt getting Payal's call?
qa.a: He likely felt shocked and scared but grateful Payal called, so he could come and stay with Anirban.

grounding: A flatmate sees a young adult who keeps working but hardly eats, sleeps a lot and says others would be better off without him, and gets him help the same night.

passage: "Neelam, you think your Ganga Mausi was always this cheerful? When I was twenty, I went to college every single day. I topped my class. People said I was so organised. But inside I felt empty, tired to my bones, and hopeless. One night I told my elder sister, 'Sometimes I think everyone would be better off if I wasn't here.' I expected her to scold. She didn't. She put down her sewing, held my hand and said, 'I am so glad you told me.' She stayed with me the whole night, and she woke our mother before dawn. That same morning they took me to a doctor, and later I saw a counsellor for many months. So listen: if you ever feel like that, you tell me that same day. Promise me."

passage: Uday, twenty-one, had worked every night shift at the call centre for three months, never missing one. His roommate had gone home for a wedding, and the flat was silent all day. On the 3 a.m. break, his team lead, Tanuja, found him staring at his cold tea. "You okay?" "I'm just tired," he said. Then, quietly: "Honestly, everyone would be better off if I was gone." Tanuja didn't leave. She sat down beside him. "Thank you for telling me. I'm staying right here." With his agreement she called the mental health helpline on speaker, and they talked through it together. Then she messaged his brother and arranged for Uday to stay at a colleague's place. The next afternoon, she went with him to see the company counsellor.

passage: Salma, twenty, went to every lecture at her Mumbai college. She handed in every assignment. At home she smiled at dinner. At night, in the room she shared with her older sister Zeenat, she lay awake feeling hollow. One night she said into the dark, "Apa, sometimes I think you'd all be better off without me." Zeenat switched on the lamp and came to sit on her bed. "I'm really glad you told me. I'm not going anywhere." She listened for a long time. Then she said, "We're telling Ammi now, together." They woke their mother. Ammi held Salma while Zeenat called a helpline, and they stayed with her all night. The next morning, the three of them went to the college counsellor.

qa.a: She shared a room with her older sister Zeenat.

passage:
"You came to every lecture this week, Saurabh. Top marks in the quiz, too," Kamal said, as they sat on the hostel steps at four o'clock.
"Yeah. I come. I sit. I go back to the room and lie there."
"You look exhausted."
"I am. Everything feels empty. Honestly, sometimes I think everyone would be happier if I just wasn't here."
Kamal went still. He turned to face Saurabh. "I'm really glad you told me. I need to ask you straight. Are you thinking of ending your life?"
"I don't know. I think about it."
"Okay. Thank you for being honest. I'm not leaving you. The counselling centre is open right now. Will you walk there with me?"
Saurabh stared at the ground. "What if they think I'm dramatic?"
"They won't. And I'll sit with you the whole time."
Saurabh nodded. Kamal stood up and held out his hand, and they walked over together.

qa.q: Where were Saurabh and Kamal sitting?
qa.a: On the hostel steps at four o'clock.

qa.q: How was Saurabh feeling behind his good attendance and marks?
qa.a: He felt empty, exhausted and hopeless, even thinking everyone would be happier if he wasn't there.

qa.q: Why was Kamal's response the right one?
qa.a: He took the words seriously, asked directly, stayed with Saurabh and went with him to the counselling centre right away instead of leaving it for later.

qa.q: How might Kamal be feeling as he asks the direct question?
qa.a: He is probably frightened and shaken, but he stays calm because he cares and wants Saurabh safe.
